To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the potential of space-borne CO2 measurements for monitoring the emissions of point and area sources is strongly dependent on the emission budgets, the wind speed, the spatial and temporal resolutions of the satellite images, and on the prior flux uncertainties, and that this potential can be quantified by uncertainty reductions from prior knowledge.

the atmospheric signal of CO2 from point sources is detectable at the scale of the satellite footprint, but that the overlap of plumes from neighboring sources and natural fluxes can significantly degrade the ability to monitor the emissions of individual point sources.

the potential of the satellite data for monitoring emissions is highly sensitive to the wind speed, and that it depends on the emission budget, the prior uncertainty and the spatial extent of the emissions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an inversion system to quantify the potential of satellite data on the monitoring of CO2 emissions.
the potential of space-based CO2 measurements to provide new insights into the anthropogenic emissions at the regional to continental scale.
the assessment of the capabilities of spaceborne CO 2 observations to constrain the emissions of the most intense sources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the potential of satellite measurements to monitor CO2 emissions depends on the emission budgets, the wind speed and the prior uncertainties, and is also strongly dependent on the targeted scale.
the monitoring capabilities are limited to large cities and point sources, with the exception of some regions with very high emissions.
the potential of space-based XCO2 measurements to constrain the emissions at a given scale is highly dependent on the wind speed, on the prior uncertainties and on the emission budget.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, with a perfect knowledge of the atmospheric transport, the satellite data would be able to monitor the annual CO2 emissions of the Paris area with a precision of ~1 MtC year−1 and of the Paris region with a precision of 1.5 MtC years−1.

the satellite data can be used to monitor the CO2 emissions of large cities or large power plants, and to monitor the regional budgets of the diffuse emissions, but not to monitor separately the emissions of small cities or small power plants.

a 50 % UR is achievable for a large ensemble of cities and power plants, but only for the budgets of their emissions during the hours before the satellite overpass, and that this UR is strongly dependent on the wind conditions and the emission budget.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, with the current satellite technology, spaceborne CO2 observations can only monitor a fraction of the anthropogenic emissions at the local to national scale.
the potential of satellite data for the monitoring of CO2 emissions at regional scales is highly sensitive to the prior uncertainties and to the wind speed.

the monitoring of emissions with a single overpass will not be able to achieve the same precision as the one of a long time series of observations, and the results of the inversion system are strongly dependent on the prior uncertainties of the natural flux estimates.
